section_summary: This section documents American and Japanese efforts in mid-1937 to suppress narcotics smuggling, especially following the Heian Maru seizure and the arrest of Toshiteru Nonaka. Much of the correspondence concerns a diplomatic dispute over Treasury representatives conducting investigations or contacting local Japanese authorities without going through the American Embassy and Japanese Foreign Office. The section also details Japanese customs and shipping-company surveillance at major ports, plans for a Japanese police official to study American enforcement methods, and proposals to strengthen Japanese narcotics penalties.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Geneva telegram concerning Far Eastern narcotics and the Heian Maru seizure
subfiles.doc_type: departmental note with enclosed telegram paraphrase
subfiles.about: Transmits Harry J. Anslinger's report on the Opium Advisory Committee and Japanese arrests arising from the Heian Maru seizure.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Geneva telegram: Anslinger reports American, Canadian and Egyptian condemnation of narcotics conditions in Japanese-controlled areas; Japanese police arrested Nonaka at Dairen and Saito at Kobe over drugs seized at Seattle.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese raids following the Geneva reprimand
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Geneva report concerning Japanese raids in concessions after criticism at Geneva.
subfiles.summary: File note on a June 16, 1937 Geneva communication about Japanese consular detectives' raids after the Geneva reprimand.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Japanese anti-narcotics raids
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese information that Japan began raids and seizures after denunciations of Japanese drug traffic at Geneva.
subfiles.summary: Chinese representatives at Geneva report Japan began a vigorous North China anti-trafficking campaign and its consular detectives raided concessions, seizing 150,000 yuan of opium, after criticism at the Opium Advisory Committee.

subfiles.title: File note on congratulating Japan for Nonaka's apprehension
subfiles.about: Summarizes instructions to tell Japanese authorities that the Treasury Department welcomed Nonaka's apprehension.
subfiles.summary: File note on telegram no. 88 to Japan: Treasury's gratification at the arrest of Toshiteru Nonaka in the Heian Maru case.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese requests for evidence in the Nonaka case
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Tokyo telegram requesting morphine samples, evidence and the seized container for Nonaka's prosecution.
subfiles.summary: File note on Grew's telegram no. 163: Japan asks for a morphine sample, other evidence and the seized container in the Nonaka case.

subfiles.title: Telegram on evidence requested for the Nonaka prosecution
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese requests for physical evidence to examine and prosecute Nonaka and his accomplices.
subfiles.summary: Grew says Japanese authorities need time to examine Nonaka and accomplices and request a morphine sample, further evidence and the seized container by express.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japan Advertiser article on the Tanda arrests
subfiles.about: Forwards a newspaper report about nine Chinese arrested aboard the British freighter Tanda for opium smuggling.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury a May 20, 1937 Japan Advertiser item on the arrest of nine Chinese aboard the British freighter Tanda.

subfiles.title: Nine Chinese Arrested Aboard British Ship on Charge of Smuggling and Selling Opium
subfiles.about: Reports arrests and an alleged opium-smoking operation aboard the British freighter Tanda, along with statistics on drug addiction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ten disguised Yokohama policemen arrested nine Chinese aboard the Tanda; the chief painter allegedly rented quarters for smoking and smuggled opium for two years. Clipping also covers action against doctors and rising addict numbers.

subfiles.title: File note on floating corpses at Tientsin
subfiles.about: Records a Japan Chronicle clipping about floating corpses found in a river at Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: File note on a Treasury communication enclosing a Japan Chronicle clipping about floating corpses in a Tientsin river.

subfiles.title: File note on shipment of evidence for the Nonaka case
subfiles.about: Records the dispatch of morphine hydrochloride and a seized tub for use in prosecuting Nonaka.
subfiles.summary: File note: twenty-five grams of morphine hydrochloride enclosed for the Nonaka prosecution, and Treasury sending one seized Heian Maru tub by express.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding a Kobe report on narcotics investigations
subfiles.about: Forwards Martin G. Scott's June 3 report from Kobe for use in discussions about narcotics cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Graves sends Hornbeck the Treasury representative's Kobe report, pointing to its last paragraph on the new Kobe Customs narcotics detail.

subfiles.title: Report on the apprehension of Toshiteru Nonaka and Kobe Customs narcotics unit
subfiles.from: Martin G. Scott, Treasury Attaché, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports Nonaka's arrest, the investigation of his gang and establishment of a six-officer narcotics unit at Kobe Customs.
subfiles.summary: Scott reports Nonaka was arrested at Dairen May 28 and returned to Kobe, associates traced across several cities, and Kobe Customs created a six-officer narcotics force.

subfiles.title: Telegram proposing categories for handling narcotics inquiries in Japan
subfiles.about: Reviews a Kobe plan dividing narcotics cases among the Treasury representative, consulate and embassy and asks for instructions.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays Scott's three-category plan: Treasury handles trivial checks, the Consulate small investigations, the Embassy delicate cases; the Embassy wants more than trivial matters centralized, as Japan wants requests routed through it. Instructions requested.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting expedited report on Kobe narcotics cooperation
subfiles.about: Requests prompt reporting on Kobe Customs' narcotics detail and its information-sharing with the Treasury representative.
subfiles.summary: Department says Kobe's Treasury representative reported six customs officers on drug traffic and police cooperation, and asks the Embassy to expedite its requested report.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum for Hornbeck on Tokyo telegram No. 178
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs staff
subfiles.about: Introduces an attached analysis of Tokyo's proposed narcotics-investigation procedure and recommends following the Embassy's position.
subfiles.summary: Routing note for Hornbeck on Tokyo telegram 178: Kobe wanted explicit guidance and Japan long wanted official-assistance requests via the Embassy; recommends accepting its advice to centralize non-trivial cases.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo telegram No. 178 and direct exchanges with Japanese officials
subfiles.about: Analyzes prior rules governing narcotics inquiries in Japan and warns against direct contacts and payments to informers.
subfiles.summary: Morlock traces instructions since 1933 requiring consular narcotics requests to pass through the Embassy, including the Cheribon Maru precedent and the Embassy's April 1937 order. He notes that Anslinger understood all exchanges under the 1928 agreement to go through the Embassy, notwithstanding broader 1937 guidance permitting direct exchanges elsewhere. Morlock concludes that existing procedures in Japan should remain and warns that providing the Kobe Treasury representative with money for informers could conflict with Japan's stated objections to foreign officials paying rewards.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese complaint in the Nonaka case
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Tokyo telegram alleging that Treasury activity delayed the Nonaka prosecution and recommending consultations.
subfiles.summary: File note on Grew's telegram no. 212: Japan's Foreign Office says Kobe's Treasury representative delayed the Nonaka prosecution; Grew suggests bringing the officers to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recommending delay pending Fuller's return
subfiles.about: Reports preparation of drafts on State–Treasury cooperation and recommends waiting for Fuller before proceeding.
subfiles.summary: Morlock drafted a letter to Graves and a reply to Tokyo, and recommends no further action until Fuller returns by July 26.

subfiles.title: Suggested telephone statement to Harold N. Graves
subfiles.doc_type: internal memorandum and draft talking points
subfiles.about: Supplies Hornbeck with proposed language for updating Graves on the unresolved narcotics-cooperation issue.
subfiles.summary: Suggested statement for Hornbeck to Graves: the Department asked Tokyo to reconsider April 1937 restrictions and got the Kobe three-category plan; consulting Fuller is needed before further discussion.

subfiles.title: Letter on the Kobe narcotics dispute and proposed Tokyo consultation
subfiles.about: Asks Treasury to defer broader discussions and jointly authorize its Kobe representative to attend a Tokyo conference.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck tells Graves study awaits Fuller's return, but a new Japanese Foreign Office complaint makes consultation urgent; he asks if Treasury will let Scott attend a Tokyo meeting with Kobe and Yokohama officers.

subfiles.title: Treasury response agreeing to Tokyo consultation
subfiles.about: Agrees to hold the broader issue in abeyance and authorize Treasury Representative Scott to attend the Tokyo conference.
subfiles.summary: Graves agrees to wait for Fuller's return on the general question and will authorize Scott to go to Tokyo at the same time as State.

subfiles.title: Letter confirming Treasury's instructions to Scott
subfiles.about: Reports that Customs ordered Martin G. Scott to Tokyo to discuss new narcotics-investigation procedures.
subfiles.summary: Graves quotes Customs' telegram directing Scott to go to Tokyo at the Embassy's convenience to discuss new narcotics investigation procedure.

subfiles.title: Telegram authorizing Kobe and Yokohama officers to attend Tokyo conference
subfiles.about: Authorizes travel by consular officers for the narcotics conference and requests a report of its results.
subfiles.summary: Embassy authorized to send one officer each from Kobe and Yokohama to Tokyo for consultation, with travel expenses, and to cable the conference's conclusions.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting the Tokyo narcotics conference and Japanese objections
subfiles.about: Reports the conference's decision to centralize investigations after Japan protested direct activities by Treasury personnel.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Japan strongly objected to Treasury investigative work; he told Treasury staff to refer investigations to the Embassy, since visits tied to Tensaka and Nonaka allegedly helped Nonaka escape to Manchuria, and warns of demands to limit Treasury work.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the 1928 and 1929 narcotics agreements with Japan
subfiles.about: Explains the agreements requiring narcotics information exchanges to pass through the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on the July 6, 1928 executive agreement and 1929 supplement on exchanging narcotics information through the Japanese Foreign Office; in 1933 all requests for Japanese investigation went through the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Despatch on cooperation of the Kobe Treasury representative with local authorities
subfiles.about: Forwards Consul Scott's explanation of the six-officer Kobe Customs narcotics detail.
subfiles.summary: Grew responds to the Department's inquiry about Treasury reports of a special six-person Japanese narcotics detail and direct information from local police. He encloses Consul Winthrop R. Scott's letter and memorandum explaining the local customs reorganization.

subfiles.title: Consul Scott's letter on the Kobe Customs reorganization
subfiles.about: Explains that Kobe Customs merely reassigned six existing officers and argues that the Treasury report had been overinterpreted.
subfiles.summary: Consul Scott says six existing Criminal Section members were assigned to narcotics on May 17 with no staff increase; the Treasury representative may have received customs information directly, a minor matter.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Kobe Customs narcotics personnel
subfiles.to: Winthrop R. Scott and American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes the organization and duties of Kobe Customs officers assigned to narcotics investigations.
subfiles.summary: Before May 17 any of sixteen Criminal Section members could handle narcotics cases; six were then assigned exclusively to them, acting on police-section information.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting Japanese customs narcotics procedures
subfiles.about: Forwards a voluntarily supplied Japanese statement on customs supervision of narcotics traffic.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses a translated July 21 letter from the Director of the Japanese Treaty Bureau. The letter transmits a Finance Department statement describing newly adopted customs procedures for supervising narcotics traffic.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Japanese customs procedures
subfiles.about: Sends the American Embassy a statement of Japanese customs procedures for narcotics supervision.
subfiles.summary: Mitani forwards a Japanese Department of Finance statement on customs procedures to First Secretary McGurk.

subfiles.title: Statement of Japanese customs measures against narcotics smuggling
subfiles.to: Japanese Foreign Office and American Embassy
subfiles.about: Details anti-smuggling organization and inspection practices at Yokohama, Kobe, Osaka, Nagasaki, Moji and Hakodate.
subfiles.summary: The statement describes special officers, suspect lists, passenger and vessel inspections, cooperation with police and procurators, and reporting systems at Japan's principal customs houses. Yokohama focused especially on China–North America traffic, while Kobe assigned six officers and created a smuggling-suppression section. Osaka, Nagasaki, Moji and Hakodate adopted port-specific surveillance of vessels, crews, merchants, cargo and travelers.

subfiles.title: Telegram on proposed visit by a Japanese police official
subfiles.about: Reports Japan's proposal to send a Metropolitan Police officer to study American customs work on the Pacific Coast.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese Foreign Office official asks whether the U.S. would welcome a Metropolitan Police officer to observe anti-smuggling methods; the Embassy replies favorably.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese customs-control statement to Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew's despatch and the Japanese statement on narcotics controls at six major customs ports.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury despatch No. 2512 on recent customs measures at Japanese ports.

subfiles.title: Telegram identifying Shinji Taniguchi's American study visit
subfiles.about: Reports that Shinji Taniguchi will visit Seattle and the United States to study narcotics-control methods.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office names Shinji Taniguchi of the Metropolitan Police Health Section as the visiting official, due at Seattle September 21; the Embassy recommends informing Customs.

subfiles.title: Letter notifying Treasury of Taniguchi's visit
subfiles.about: Notifies Treasury that Shinji Taniguchi will visit the United States to observe American narcotics enforcement.
subfiles.summary: Moore reviews the Japanese Foreign Office's August inquiry about sending a police official to the Pacific Coast and the Embassy's welcoming response. He then reports that Shinji Taniguchi will arrive at Seattle on September 21 and stay through early October to study American narcotics-control methods.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting Japanese steamship and port-control measures
subfiles.about: Sends a Japanese statement on Nippon Yusen Kaisha's shipboard safeguards and surveillance at major seaports.
subfiles.summary: Instruction forwarding Japan's statement to the Opium Advisory Committee on Nippon Yusen Kaisha steamer measures and port surveillance against narcotics traffic.

subfiles.title: Mesures tendant à empêcher l'utilisation des navires transocéaniques pour le trafic illicite
subfiles.from: Japanese representative on the Opium Advisory Committee
subfiles.to: American representative on the Opium Advisory Committee
subfiles.about: Describes Nippon Yusen Kaisha and Japanese governmental measures against narcotics smuggling aboard ships and at seaports.
subfiles.summary: The statement lists daily and pre-arrival searches, dedicated searching officers, information boxes, rewards and controls over visitors, peddlers and shore leave aboard Nippon Yusen Kaisha vessels. It records the Kobe Maritime Council's 1936 decisions on reporting suspect crewmen, inspections and coordinated government action. It also describes surveillance of pharmacists, sailors, Chinese quarters and baggage, blacklists and searches before departure in Kanagawa, Osaka, Hyōgo and Fukuoka prefectures.

subfiles.title: Measures Designed to Prevent the Use of Transoceanic Steamers for the Illicit Traffic
subfiles.from: Japanese representative on the Opium Advisory Committee
subfiles.to: American representative on the Opium Advisory Committee
subfiles.about: Provides the English translation of Japanese shipping-company and port measures against illicit narcotics traffic.
subfiles.summary: The translation describes searching officers and other precautions aboard vessels on the Hong Kong–San Francisco and Kobe–Seattle routes, including the Heian Maru. It outlines Kobe Maritime Council decisions requiring shipping companies to report traffickers and improve surveillance. The final portion summarizes coordinated customs and police measures, blacklists, baggage searches and the carriage of police inspectors on ships bound for China or the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of Japanese steamship-control statement to Treasury
subfiles.about: Confidentially forwards the Japanese statement and translation on Nippon Yusen Kaisha and seaport surveillance.
subfiles.summary: State confidentially sends Treasury the Geneva statement on Nippon Yusen Kaisha shipboard measures and port surveillance, with translation.

subfiles.title: Letter on cooperation with Japan against international narcotics traffic
subfiles.about: Assesses improving Foreign Office cooperation while attributing friction in the Nonaka affair to inconsistent State and Treasury instructions.
subfiles.summary: Grew says cooperation improved through McGurk and Treaty Bureau director Mitani, who wants stronger penalties, though Mitani protested the Treasury investigation that alerted Nonaka; personnel need uniform instructions from Washington.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on a Metropolitan Police visit and stronger penalties
subfiles.about: Records Aoki's proposal for a Japanese police study visit and Mitani's campaign to strengthen Japanese narcotics laws.
subfiles.summary: Aoki asks about a Metropolitan Police official visiting Seattle and San Francisco, which McGurk welcomes, and says Mitani seeks higher narcotics penalties, possibly via Diet legislation.

subfiles.title: Letter explaining State's position on narcotics investigations in Japan
subfiles.about: Defends the Embassy's centralized procedure after Japan refused to permit Treasury representatives to conduct direct narcotics investigations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck reviews the rejected Kobe plan, the Japanese Foreign Office's complaint against Martin G. Scott and the July 29 Embassy conference. He stresses that the March 1937 State–Treasury arrangement required the assent of foreign governments and that Japan had consistently withheld permission for Treasury representatives to investigate or contact local authorities directly. He therefore endorses Grew's requirement that requests pass through the Embassy and Foreign Office, while pointing to Taniguchi's proposed visit and Mitani's legislative efforts as evidence of improving Japanese cooperation. The letter continues beyond page 320.
